unit-m3u9.title: Unit 3 · Lesson 9: Critique Reasoning
unit-m3u9.source: enVision Topic 3 textbook scan — Multiply Multi-Digit Whole Numbers (Drive)

summary.text: Lesson 3-9 of the Topic 3 textbook scan: critiquing someone else's reasoning about multiplication — checking their estimates, their calculations and whether their conclusion follows.

why.text: Explaining whether someone else's thinking is right is one of the hardest skills on a math test, and it is exactly what "Construct Arguments" and "Critique Reasoning" questions ask for.

objectives.text: Describe another person's argument and how they support it
Decide whether an estimate supports a "more than" or "less than" claim
Find and fix a flaw in a calculation
Tell a correct answer from correct reasoning

parentNote.text: The biggest idea here is that the direction of rounding decides what an estimate can prove. Two questions show opposite outcomes of the same flaw: Omar's "fewer than 18,000" turns out true but was not proved, and the "48 × 52 is more than 2,500" claim turns out false (2,496). The cargo questions are the textbook's own example with fresh numbers — rounding the heavy boxes DOWN hid 150 extra pounds. One question also shows sound reasoning (rounding down to prove "more than"), because a critique should say when an argument is right, too.

nextUp.text: Ask: which way did they round, and do the pieces add back up?

cards.def:
**Start by saying what the person is claiming and what they used to support it.**
• "She estimated 60 × 300 = 18,000 and said there are fewer than 18,000 seats."
cards.hint: Name the claim before you judge it.

cards.term: Check the direction of the estimate
cards.def:
**An estimate only supports "more than" or "less than" if it rounded the right way.**
• Both factors rounded up → overestimate. Both down → underestimate.
• One up and one down → it cannot prove either.
cards.hint: Which way did the numbers move?

cards.def:
**Look for slips: a lost zero, a wrong carry, or a number split the wrong way.**
• 400 × 63 is not (400 × 6) + (400 × 3). 63 is 60 + 3.
cards.hint: Splitting a number? The pieces must add back to it.

cards.def:
**Even a true answer can come from bad reasoning — and good-looking reasoning can be wrong.**
• Say whether the steps actually prove the claim.
cards.hint: Right answer, wrong reason, still needs fixing.

cards.def: **Critiquing means asking questions, deciding if the strategy makes sense, and looking for flaws.**

questions.q: A stadium has 62 sections with 285 seats each. Omar estimates 60 × 300 = 18,000 and says there are fewer than 18,000 seats. Does his estimate prove it?
opts: No — he rounded one number down and one up, so 18,000 could be high or low
Yes — 18,000 is an overestimate, so the real number is smaller
Yes — any estimate that ends in zeros is safe to use
No — he should have added 62 and 285 instead
questions.hint: Which way did each number get rounded?
steps: With one down and one up, the estimate could be above or below.
The real total is 17,670 — he happens to be right, but his estimate did not prove it.

ex.main: **No.** One factor went down and one went up, so 18,000 proves nothing either way.
ex.tip: His conclusion turns out true (17,670), but only an exact calculation shows that.

questions.q: An office manager works out 400 × 63 as (400 × 6) + (400 × 3) = 3,600. What is the mistake?
opts: He should have multiplied 400 by 9
He split 63 into 6 and 3 instead of 60 and 3
He should have added the parts first
There is no mistake — 3,600 is correct

ex.main: **He split 63 into 6 and 3 instead of 60 and 3.** The real product is 25,200.
ex.tip: Whenever you split a number, check that the pieces add back up to it.

questions.q: What is the correct value of 400 × 63?
Kate sold 2,085 bracelets and made $6 on each. She says, "2,000 × 6 = 12,000 and I sold more than 2,000, so I made more than $12,000." Is she right?
opts: Yes — because $12,000 is exactly what her profit comes to
No — she should have rounded 2,085 up to 3,000 to be safe
No — an estimate can never decide whether she made enough
Yes — she rounded down, so her real profit is even more than $12,000
questions.hint: Did she round 2,085 up or down?
steps: Her real profit must be more than $12,000.

ex.main: **Yes.** Rounding down gives an underestimate, and it already reaches $12,000.
ex.tip: This is sound reasoning — worth saying so when you critique, too.

questions.q: You want to know if you have ENOUGH money. Which kind of estimate of your money helps most?
opts: An underestimate, because the real amount is at least that much
An overestimate, because a bigger number is always the safer one
Any estimate at all, since they all work equally well
No estimate helps — only the exact amount can tell you
questions.hint: If your too-small estimate is enough, what about the real amount?
steps: An underestimate is smaller than what you really have.
If even that smaller amount is enough, the real amount is too.
An overestimate could make you think you have enough when you do not.

ex.main: **An underestimate.** If it is already enough, the real amount certainly is.
ex.tip: An overestimate is useful the other way round — to check that something is under a limit.

questions.q: A cargo container can hold 15,000 pounds. There are 38 boxes of 150 pounds and 45 boxes of 210 pounds. Someone estimates 40 × 150 + 45 × 200 = 15,000 and says they fit. Do they?
opts: Yes — the estimate is exactly 15,000
No — the real weight is 15,150 pounds, which is over
Yes — 38 was rounded up, so there is room to spare
No — the real weight is 25,000 pounds
questions.hint: Work out the heavier boxes exactly.
steps: That is 150 pounds over the limit.

ex.main: **No.** The real weight is 15,150 pounds — the estimate rounded 210 down and hid the extra.
ex.tip: Rounding the heavy boxes down is exactly the wrong direction when checking a limit.

questions.hint: Find 45 × 21, then put the zero on.

ex.tip: 9,000 is 45 × 200 — the estimate, not the answer.

questions.q: Which question is most useful when you critique someone's reasoning?
opts: Did they finish before everyone else in the class?
Is the final answer a big number, or a small number?
Did they write every step neatly, in pen?
Does the strategy make sense, and are the numbers right?
questions.hint: Critiquing is about the thinking, not the look of the work.
steps: A critique checks whether the method makes sense.
It also checks the calculations for slips.
Neatness and speed are not reasoning.

ex.main: **Does the strategy make sense, and are the numbers right?** That is what a critique checks.
ex.tip: Asking questions helps you understand their thinking before you decide.

questions.q: A cargo load of 38 boxes at 150 pounds and 45 boxes at 210 pounds weighs 15,150 pounds. The limit is 15,000. Raul removes two 210-pound boxes and one 150-pound box. Does it fit now?
opts: Yes — it now weighs 14,580 pounds
No — it now weighs 15,000 pounds exactly
Yes — it now weighs 14,790 pounds
No — removing boxes does not change the weight enough
questions.hint: Subtract the weight of the boxes removed.

ex.main: **Yes — 14,580 pounds.** Removing 570 pounds brings it under the limit.
ex.tip: 14,790 forgets one of the two heavy boxes.

questions.q: A student says 48 × 52 must be more than 2,500 because 50 × 50 = 2,500. Is that right?
opts: Yes — both numbers are close to 50, so the product must be more
No — rounding one up and one down can go either way; 48 × 52 is 2,496
Yes — 52 is bigger than 50, so the product has to be bigger too
No — 48 × 52 is much less than that, only about 2,000
questions.hint: Which way did 48 and 52 each move?
steps: One up and one down gives no promise.

ex.main: **No.** 48 × 52 = 2,496, just under 2,500 — mixed rounding cannot prove "more than".
ex.tip: This is the surprising one: numbers balanced around 50 give a product slightly LESS than 50 × 50.
